nameStory: The "bristly" part of this plant's name comes from the rough, spiky stems that feel scratchy to the touch - quite different from its smoother cousin, wild sarsaparilla. Like other sarsaparillas, Native Americans traditionally used the roots to make medicinal teas, though this isn't the same plant used for root beer flavoring.
description: Bristly sarsaparilla is a low-growing perennial that typically reaches 1-3 feet tall, looking somewhat like a miniature version of its woodland cousins. It has compound leaves made up of multiple small, oval leaflets with saw-toothed edges, giving it a delicate, fern-like appearance. In early summer, it produces small clusters of tiny white flowers that later develop into dark, round berries. Unlike wild sarsaparilla that prefers rich forest soils, this species thrives in sandy, open areas.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling plant rarely over 3 feet tall with distinctly rough, bristly stems that feel scratchy when you run your fingers along them

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into small, oval leaflets with sharply toothed edges; leaflets feel thin and papery compared to wild sarsaparilla's thicker leaves

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers clustered in small, rounded balls at the top of stems in June and July; individual flowers are so small they look like white dots

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dark purple-black berries in round clusters, each berry about the size of a peppercorn with a slightly wrinkled surface when ripe

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found in dry, sandy soils in open areas rather than rich forest floors - a key difference from most other sarsaparilla relatives

habitat: Look for bristly sarsaparilla in dry, sandy soils in open or partially shaded areas throughout New England. It thrives in places like sandy clearings, dry woodland edges, and areas with well-drained, nutrient-poor soils where other plants might struggle. Unlike its forest-dwelling relatives, this species prefers more exposed sites with good drainage.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, unfurling as fresh green compound leaves. The bristly stems become more noticeable as the plant puts on new growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with white flower clusters appearing in June and July, followed by developing green berries. The rough, scratchy stems are most obvious now.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to dark purple-black and leaves may turn yellowish before dropping. The persistent underground rhizome prepares for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back, but the hardy underground rhizome can survive even when exposed up to 20 inches above ground level - unusual for most perennials.

funFact: Bristly sarsaparilla has one of the most frost-hardy underground root systems in the plant world - its rhizome can survive winter temperatures even when buried less than two feet underground, something that would kill most other perennial root systems.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with wild sarsaparilla, but bristly sarsaparilla has noticeably rough, scratchy stems (wild sarsaparilla's are smooth) and grows in dry, sandy areas rather than rich forest soil. Memory trick: "Bristly likes it rough" - rough stems in rough, dry habitats.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse any of the sarsaparilla plants with the sarsaparilla flavoring used in old-fashioned root beer - that came from a completely different tropical plant. The sarsaparillas in New England are members of the ivy family, despite looking nothing like the ivy climbing up your house.
compareHints: Among New England's Aralia species, bristly sarsaparilla is the shortest and most rough-textured, preferring dry soils unlike wild sarsaparilla's forest preference or American spikenard's love of rich, moist areas. Its low growth habit and bristly stems make it unmistakable once you feel those scratchy surfaces. The small, clustered white flowers are similar to other family members but appear on a much smaller, more compact plant.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild sarsaparilla is much shorter than its Aralia relatives - bristly sarsaparilla grows taller with prickly stems, while American spikenard can reach 6 feet with multiple compound leaves and a more robust appearance.

American spikenard is much larger and more robust than its relatives - wild sarsaparilla stays close to the ground with leaves only 6-12 inches tall, while bristly sarsaparilla is covered in prickles.

Among its Aralia relatives in New England, Japanese angelica tree is by far the tallest and most tree-like, while wild sarsaparilla stays low to the ground and American spikenard is an herbaceous perennial.
Unlike its native New England Aralia cousins which are mostly low woodland herbs, Chinese angelica-tree grows much larger and lacks the thorns found on devil's walkingstick.
Among its Aralia relatives in New England, devil's walkingstick is unmistakable due to its woody, tree-like growth and extensive spines.
Japanese spikenard dwarfs its New England relatives like wild sarsaparilla and American spikenard, growing 2-3 times taller with much more robust stems.
